According to Yonhap, Samsung, SK Hynix, TSMC, Micron, and Intel are joined by key toolmakers and designers like Broadcom, Advantest, and Kioxia, alongside researchers from Stanford and UC Berkeley.
At present, testing a new manufacturing step or tool modification requires sending wafers back and forth between equipment makers in the US, Europe, or Japan and fabrication plants scattered across Asia.
Gary Dickerson, chief executive of Applied Materials, pointed out that expanding AI infrastructure introduces unprecedented technical hurdles across every layer of fabrication.
Getting a new node or HBM design into high-volume manufacturing fast is no longer just about who builds the best silicon; it comes down to who refines the tools first.
For Samsung and SK Hynix, this alliance is a strategic necessity
Samsung DS Division CTO Song Jae-hyuk noted the hub will help accelerate the transition from early technology concepts to actual fab yield.
SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung sees it as a foundation to speed up next-generation HBM, DRAM, and NAND roadmaps.
TSMC chief C.C. Wei highlighted advanced packaging as a primary focus area for their on-site research.

articles.title: South Korea’s Kospi index sinks more than 7% on semiconductor share sell-off over AI boom worries - NBC News
articles.summary: South Korea’s Kospi index sinks more than 7% on semiconductor share sell-off over AI boom worries  NBC News
articles.full_text:
HONG KONG — South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index dropped more than 7% Tuesday on a sell-off of chip shares, and Asian shares mostly declined after U.S. stocks ended mixed.
U.S. futures were also mixed, and oil prices fell as escalating tensions in the Middle East continued.
The Kospi index was down 7.4% to 5,914.35, its lowest level since late July. It reached an all-time high in June after crossing 9,000, supercharged by the global artificial intelligence boom.
Samsung Electronics fell 7.7%, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix plunged 8.8%.
Investors’ unease over the AI boom has clouded prospects. Both companies’ stocks fell following reports that the latest advances made by China’s memory chipmaker CXMT could increasingly challenge Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron Technology, the world’s biggest memory chipmakers.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.5% to 67,292.39. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron fell 6.6%. SoftBank Group, an OpenAI investor, lost 8%.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1% to 24,033.51. The Shanghai Composite index was 1.1% lower at 3,754.82.
Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 edged down 0.2% to 8,767.40.
Taiwan’s Taiex fell 1.9%, with its leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., down 1.6%.
On Monday, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 edged down 0.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.4%, and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite declined 0.4%.
Chip-related shares traded lower. Nvidia was down 1.3%. Advanced Micro Devices, or AMD, was 2.3% lower. Micron Technology lost 3.9%. Broadcom fell 1.9%.
Investors are also watching this week’s earnings announcements by major firms including big banks, with Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo reporting results.
Oil prices dropped more than 1%. Brent crude, the international standard, fell 1.4% to $105.20 a barrel. That’s still higher than the roughly $72 per barrel in late February, before the Iran war.
Benchmark U.S. crude was down 1.5% to $92.34 a barrel.
“The market is more concerned over recent developments in the Middle East, with Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and the lingering risks to oil flows from the Persian Gulf,” wrote ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey in a commentary Tuesday.
The U.S. dollar fell to 158.26 Japanese yen from 158.61 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1175, up from $1.1155.

articles.title: Korean chip giants join $5bn global semiconductor R&D Center - 매일경제
articles.summary: Korean chip giants join $5bn global semiconductor R&D Center  매일경제
articles.full_text:
Samsung Electronics Co. and SK hynix Inc. have joined a global semiconductor research and development (R&D) initiative led by U.S. equipment maker Applied Materials Inc., which unveiled a $5 billion facility in Sunnyvale, California, on Monday, local time.
The Equipment and Process Innovation and Commercialization (EPIC) Center is the world’s largest facility dedicated to collaborative R&D of semiconductor manufacturing equipment and process technologies. The 55,700 square-meter facility includes 16,200 square meters of advanced cleanroom space.
“As artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure expands, the demand for high-performance computing is creating unprecedented complexity across semiconductor manufacturing technology development roadmaps,” said Gary Dickerson, chief executive officer (CEO) of Applied Materials, emphasizing the need for a new approach to collaboration in semiconductor technology development and commercialization.
The EPIC Center aims to shorten the time required to develop and commercialize next-generation semiconductor technologies by integrating everything from semiconductor materials research to equipment and process development and pilot production under one roof.
Founding partners include Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, TSMC, Intel Corp., and Micron Technology Inc. Innovation partners include Broadcom Inc., Advantest Corp., SCREEN Holdings Co., Kioxia Holdings Corp., and BE Semiconductor Industries N.V. (Besi), along with Stanford University and the University of California, Berkeley.
Participating companies expressed expectations that the center would accelerate the development and commercialization of next-generation technologies.
“Through EPIC, we will further accelerate the entire process from the development of innovative technologies to their refinement and real-world application,” said Song Jei- hyuck, chief technology officer (CTO) of Samsung Electronics‘ Device Solutions (DS) division.
SK hynix President and CEO Kwak Noh-jung expressed his company’s intention to address major technological transitions across high-bandwidth memory (HBM), DRAM and NAND through collaboration with AMAT.
C.C. Wei, chairman and CEO of TSMC, highlighted the prospect of gaining early access to next-generation semiconductor equipment technologies and advancing areas such as advanced packaging.
Sanjay Mehrotra, chairman and CEO of Micron, anticipated that the collaboration would help accelerate the transition from next-generation memory research to large-scale mass production.

Asia news for October 12, 2026: China-EU trade negotiations, India’s inflation and protests, North Korean missiles, and Singapore’s AI warnings
NetNewsLedger International News | Monday, October 12, 2026
THUNDER BAY, ON — Asia’s largest economies are facing a week of growing political, economic and security challenges as trade disputes, inflation, artificial intelligence and military tensions reshape the region.
For Monday, October 12, 2026, the leading developments across Singapore, China, India and Japan include a new China-European Union trade arrangement, widespread political protests in India, North Korean ballistic missile launches near Japan, and warnings from Singapore’s leaders about the impact of artificial intelligence on employment.
The news matters far beyond Asia. Decisions being made in Beijing, New Delhi, Singapore and Tokyo could influence Canadian manufacturers, Ontario’s critical minerals industry, global investment and the cost of imported goods.
For Northwestern Ontario, where mining, forestry, transportation and international trade remain essential parts of the economy, developments in Asian markets deserve close attention.
Singapore: Artificial Intelligence, Economic Growth and Public Health
1. President Tharman warns artificial intelligence is threatening entry-level jobs
Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam delivered a warning at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Monday.
Speaking about the growing use of artificial intelligence, Tharman said governments need to address a decline in demand for workers entering the labour market.
New university graduates may be among the first to experience the change, as businesses turn to automated systems for tasks previously handled by junior employees.
The Singapore president also warned that AI could widen economic divisions between richer countries and developing nations.
The concern is not simply that existing jobs will disappear. It is that young workers could lose the entry-level opportunities that traditionally allow them to gain experience and advance into better-paying careers.
The issue has become an international economic challenge as companies invest heavily in AI systems that can handle research, financial analysis, customer service and administrative work.
2. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong calls for AI to strengthen society
Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong is also urging businesses and educators to use artificial intelligence without sacrificing the development of human skills.
Wong said Singapore must protect basic learning in schools and ensure employers continue training and mentoring junior employees.
His government’s approach places emphasis on retraining, fair treatment of displaced workers and regional digital cooperation through the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
The message is that Singapore wants to benefit from AI-driven growth without allowing technology to weaken education or eliminate pathways into employment.
3. Singapore faces an important monetary policy decision on October 14
The Monetary Authority of Singapore is expected to tighten monetary policy when it releases its next decision on Wednesday, October 14.
All 10 economists surveyed by Reuters before the meeting expected further tightening.
Singapore’s economy has benefited from strong investment in technology and AI infrastructure, but rising energy prices and food supply risks have created fresh inflation concerns.
Unlike the Bank of Canada, Singapore’s central bank primarily manages monetary conditions through the exchange rate rather than a conventional policy interest rate.
Economists are watching whether the authority will allow the Singapore dollar to appreciate more quickly to help control the cost of imported goods.
4. Smoke and haze raise health concerns
Singapore is also dealing with unhealthy air quality linked to regional haze.
The government has activated medical subsidy measures beginning October 12 to help eligible residents seek treatment for haze-related health problems.
The environmental problem has affected transportation, with Malaysian carrier Firefly cancelling flights between Seletar and Subang airports as a safety precaution.
The situation illustrates how air pollution crossing international borders can affect public health, business operations and transportation across Southeast Asia.
Why Singapore matters to Canada: Singapore is a major financial, shipping and technology centre. Its experience with AI, inflation and regional trade offers an early view of challenges that Canadian businesses and governments are also confronting.
China: European Trade Negotiations, Taiwan and Growing Economic Pressures
1. China and European Union reach arrangement on hybrid vehicle exports
One of Monday’s biggest international business developments comes from trade negotiations between Beijing and Brussels.
China’s Ministry of Commerce announced the outcome of extensive consultations with the European Union over trade in hybrid and electric vehicles.
The arrangement addresses European concerns about the growing volume of Chinese-made vehicles entering its markets while attempting to provide Chinese exporters with greater certainty.
European officials have indicated the measures could sharply reduce Chinese hybrid vehicle shipments to the EU. China says the arrangement must avoid discrimination and provide a predictable framework for exporters.
The outcome follows three months of negotiations involving senior trade officials.
However, the agreement does not resolve every trade dispute between China and Europe.
The broader issue remains competition between China’s rapidly expanding automotive industry and European manufacturers facing significant pressure from lower-cost imports.
Why this matters to Ontario
Ontario’s automobile manufacturing industry is closely linked to the North American market, but competition from China has become a major international issue.
Chinese electric vehicle manufacturers have developed substantial capacity in battery technology, vehicle assembly and supply chains.
The European arrangement could influence how other governments consider tariffs, import restrictions and industrial policy.
For Northern Ontario, the longer-term implications include investment in nickel, lithium, graphite and other minerals used in batteries and advanced manufacturing.
A significant shift in where electric vehicles are manufactured can influence which mining and processing projects attract investment.
2. Beijing imposes sanctions on officials from two countries that recognize Taiwan
China announced sanctions Monday against officials from Paraguay and Belize over their countries’ diplomatic relationships with Taiwan.
The sanctions target Paraguay’s Communications Minister Gustavo Villate and Belize’s Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca.
Measures include travel restrictions covering Hong Kong and Macau and prohibitions on cooperation with Chinese organizations.
Taiwan condemned the move as interference in the sovereign foreign-policy decisions of other countries.
Beijing considers Taiwan part of China and has worked for years to reduce the number of countries maintaining official diplomatic relations with Taipei.
The sanctions are largely symbolic, but they underscore continuing diplomatic tensions surrounding Taiwan’s international recognition.
3. China’s growing debt raises questions about its economic model
A separate economic analysis published Monday by The Wall Street Journal examines the mounting debt associated with China’s investments in manufacturing, technology, infrastructure and local government projects.
China has continued to prioritize industrial expansion and technological leadership, even as weak domestic demand and difficulties in the property market put pressure on economic growth.
High borrowing levels have raised concerns about whether some investments will generate enough revenue to repay their costs.
The challenge for Beijing is balancing support for strategically important industries with the need to strengthen household consumption and financial stability.
China’s ability to manage its debt will affect global demand for minerals, construction materials and industrial equipment.
4. China continues investing in artificial intelligence infrastructure
Chinese companies and governments are accelerating investment in computing facilities designed to support large-scale AI applications.
State news agency Xinhua reported Monday on the development of so-called token factories, facilities that provide the computing capacity required to run AI services at scale.
The expansion reflects China’s ambition to compete with the United States in artificial intelligence and the infrastructure behind it.
Such growth requires advanced chips, electricity, cooling systems, data centres and substantial capital investment.
For Northwestern Ontario, the important question is whether this global technology expansion creates sustainable demand for copper, nickel and other mineral inputs, and how much of that opportunity Canadian producers can capture.
India: Mass Protests, Rising Inflation and Renewed Canada-India Diplomacy

One of India’s biggest stories Monday is a growing protest movement challenging the country’s election authorities.
Thousands of demonstrators marched in New Delhi demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The protests centre on allegations that changes to electoral rolls removed large numbers of voters and unfairly benefited Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.
Opposition groups and youth activists have accused election officials of undermining democratic accountability.

articles.title: South Korea's Honam Semiconductor Power Grid: Samsung, SK Hynix to Bear 80% of 1.4 Trillion Won Cost - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: South Korea's Honam Semiconductor Power Grid: Samsung, SK Hynix to Bear 80% of 1.4 Trillion Won Cost  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) confirmed that Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix will bear 80% of the 1.4 trillion won (approximately $1.1 billion) power grid construction cost required for South Korea's Honam semiconductor industrial complex. KEPCO CEO Kim Dong-chul confirmed the cost-sharing structure during a National Assembly audit by the Trade, Industry, Energy, SMEs, and Startups Committee on the 12th, explaining that it is premised on the assumption that government support under the Semiconductor Special Act will not be provided.
Responding to a question from People Power Party lawmaker Kim Do-eup about transmission facility budgets, Kim said, "KEPCO's share is less than 20%," adding that "Samsung and SK Hynix are set to bear the remainder." When lawmaker Cho Ji-yeon asked again whether it was correct that the private sector would shoulder 80% of the 1.4 trillion won, Kim confirmed, "That is correct."
He noted that the power grid in question is a dedicated line for Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, saying "the consumers are required to bear the cost." However, the Semiconductor Special Act stipulates that the national and local governments may cover 50–100% of total project costs for industrial infrastructure construction and operation needed for clusters. Kim elaborated, "If the government provides support, that is how it would work. If there is no support under the Semiconductor Special Act, KEPCO, Samsung, and SK Hynix will share the burden according to their electricity usage ratios."
During the audit, lawmaker Cho pointed out, "The president himself said the government would take responsibility for power and water," adding, "Even though the special act requires the government to bear more than 50%, KEPCO says it will cover only 20% and the companies will pay the rest." She criticized, "Ultimately, this is telling companies to invest and build all the power infrastructure themselves. They've twisted not just the companies' right arm but their left arm as well."
Prepayment Proposal Unrelated to Honam Semiconductor
Kim also made clear that the electricity bill prepayment proposal was not directly related to the Honam semiconductor complex construction. When lawmaker Yoon Han-hong asked whether KEPCO had demanded prepayment from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix for the Honam semiconductor construction, Kim emphasized the timing showed no connection, saying, "KEPCO proposed the prepayment to the companies in March–April, while the decision to build the Honam semiconductor complex was made at the end of June."
Earlier this year, KEPCO proposed that Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix prepay 25 trillion won (approximately $18.8 billion) in electricity bills for the period from 2027 to 2031, to be paid in advance over one year. This amounts to roughly five years' worth of electricity bills for each company based on what they paid last year. When lawmaker Yoon suggested the two companies likely rejected the prepayment due to semiconductor industry uncertainty and the burden of massive capital outflows, Kim replied, "That is correct."
The KEPCO bond issuance limit was identified as the backdrop for the prepayment proposal. Kim Jae-gun, KEPCO's vice president of power systems, explained, "Our current bond ratio is 5x, and we need to reduce it to 2x by the end of 2027. We proposed this to resolve the issue on our own." CEO Kim also said, "From KEPCO's perspective, maintaining the bond issuance multiple within 2x is indeed the biggest challenge."
KEPCO's bond issuance limit is, in principle, twice the sum of its capital and reserves. However, due to the funding crunch from massive losses in 2022, the KEPCO Act was amended to temporarily allow issuance up to 5x until the end of 2027. Kim indicated that an electricity rate hike will be unavoidable once this special allowance expires.
When Democratic Party lawmaker Chung Jin-wook asked about plans to secure funding for power grid investment, Kim responded, "If the bond issuance multiple is reduced from 5x to 2x at the end of 2027, KEPCO will no longer be able to issue bonds. While self-help efforts are necessary, I believe a minimum electricity rate increase will be needed." When lawmaker Chung mentioned the need for government fiscal input, Kim nodded in agreement.
Currently, household electricity rates have been frozen for 14 consecutive quarters, and industrial rates for 8 consecutive quarters. While rate adjustments have been delayed, KEPCO's total debt has surpassed 200 trillion won (approximately $150.1 billion), with daily interest costs reaching the 10 billion won (approximately $7.5 million) range.
Power Grid Investment Remains Top Priority
Despite the financial burden, Kim stated that power grid investment will remain the top priority. "Although financial conditions are difficult in many ways, we are placing power grid investment at the highest priority," he said.
Regarding the need for redundancy in power grids supplying the Honam semiconductor industrial complex and other areas, Kim explained that the grids currently managed by KEPCO are already configured bidirectionally, so if a failure occurs on one side, the other grid can temporarily compensate. "There are almost no single-line grids currently managed by KEPCO," Kim added.
Meanwhile, regarding the government's Public Official Ethics Committee decision to deny employment approval for former South Jeolla Province Governor Kim Young-rok, who had been mentioned as a potential successor, Kim briefly stated, "I understand there were issues in the subsequent personnel process."
The Honam semiconductor industrial complex is a region where Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix have announced large-scale investments, and infrastructure expansion including power and water has been identified as a key variable determining the project's success. SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won visited the Honam semiconductor site on the 9th and repeatedly raised power and water supply issues.
The cost-sharing structure revealed during this National Assembly audit could change depending on whether support under the Semiconductor Special Act is provided. If the national and local governments cover 50–100% of total project costs under the special act, the burden on companies and KEPCO would be significantly reduced. Conversely, if special act support is not provided, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix would have to bear more than 1.1 trillion won (approximately $825.7 million) of the 1.4 trillion won total.

articles.summary: Wafer Manufacturing Equipment Market To 2035: AI Chip Demand Drives Growth - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Applied Materials
Largest WFE supplier
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Wafer Manufacturing Equipment market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global wafer manufacturing equipment market is entering a structurally transformative decade, with the forecast period 2026-2035 shaped by the semiconductor industry's response to AI, high-performance computing, and pervasive connectivity. Wafer manufacturing equipment encompasses the capital systems used in deposition, etching, lithography, cleaning, and metrology—the core process steps that convert bare silicon into finished wafers. Demand is bifurcating: leading-edge logic and foundry nodes require extreme ultraviolet lithography, atomic layer deposition, and high-aspect-ratio etch tools, while mature nodes face accelerated refresh cycles to improve throughput and energy efficiency.
The procurement model is shifting from one-time capital expenditure to lifecycle partnerships, with service, consumables, and upgrades now a majority of vendor profitability. Geopolitical fragmentation is creating parallel equipment ecosystems, as export controls compel separate capacity build-outs in different regions. Supply chain control—especially in EUV light sources and precision optics—has become a competitive moat.
This report provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of market size, segmentation, demand drivers, competitive dynamics, and regional outlook through 2035, designed for component manufacturers, system suppliers, OEMs, distributors, investors, and strategic entrants.
The baseline scenario for the wafer manufacturing equipment market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates sustained expansion, with a compound annual growth rate of 6.2% and a market index reaching 182 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook assumes no severe global recession, continued semiconductor content growth, and a gradual easing of supply chain bottlenecks. The primary demand engine is the build-out of leading-edge logic and foundry capacity to support AI accelerators, high-performance computing, and advanced mobile processors. Memory makers are also investing in 3D NAND and DRAM scaling, though with cyclical pauses.
Mature node equipment demand is supported by automotive, industrial, and IoT applications, where chipmakers are refreshing older fabs to improve energy efficiency and automation compatibility. Regionally, Asia-Pacific remains the largest market, with China aggressively expanding domestic capacity despite export controls, while North America and Europe increase their share through incentive-backed fab projects. The competitive landscape is concentrated among a few integrated platform leaders, but niche opportunities exist in metrology, cleaning, and advanced packaging-adjacent tools. Risks include geopolitical escalation, a slowdown in AI capital expenditure, and talent shortages.
Overall, the market is poised for robust growth, with recurring revenue streams providing resilience against capital spending cycles.
Foundry and logic manufacturers are the largest end-users of wafer manufacturing equipment, accounting for nearly half of global demand. This segment is driven by the continuous push to smaller nodes, with 3nm and 2nm production ramping up through 2026-2035. The rise of AI accelerators, CPUs, and GPUs requires advanced lithography, deposition, and etch tools capable of atomic-level precision. Demand-side indicators include fab construction announcements, wafer starts per month, and capital expenditure guidance from TSMC, Samsung, and Intel. As leading-edge nodes become more complex, the number of process steps increases, raising equipment intensity per wafer.
The transition to gate-all-around transistors and backside power delivery will further boost demand for selective deposition and high-aspect-ratio etch. Foundries are also expanding capacity in the US and Europe, supported by government subsidies, which will sustain equipment orders. However, cyclical pauses and geopolitical tensions may cause short-term volatility. Overall, this segment will remain the primary growth engine, with a focus on tools that enable yield and performance at scale. Current trend: Growing share due to AI and HPC demand.
Major trends: Ramp of 3nm and 2nm gate-all-around nodes, Backside power delivery adoption, Regional fab build-outs in US and Europe, Increasing process step count per wafer, and AI-driven process control and yield management.
Representative participants: TSMC, Samsung Foundry, Intel Foundry, GlobalFoundries, and SMIC.
Memory manufacturers, including DRAM and NAND flash producers, represent a quarter of wafer manufacturing equipment demand. This segment is highly cyclical but is undergoing structural growth due to data center, AI, and edge storage requirements. 3D NAND makers are transitioning to higher layer counts (200+ layers), which demands advanced etch and deposition tools for high-aspect-ratio structures. DRAM scaling is approaching physical limits, pushing adoption of EUV lithography and new materials. Demand-side indicators include bit growth, capital expenditure plans from Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron, and inventory levels.
The memory segment is also seeing increased equipment intensity as 3D NAND requires more deposition and etch steps per wafer. Through 2035, memory makers will invest in capacity expansions and technology upgrades, though periodic oversupply may temper growth. The shift to DDR5 and HBM for AI servers is a key driver for DRAM equipment. Overall, this segment offers significant opportunities for equipment suppliers that can address high-aspect-ratio etch and conformal deposition challenges. Current trend: Cyclical but growing, driven by 3D NAND and DRAM scaling.
Major trends: 3D NAND layer count exceeding 200 layers, DRAM adoption of EUV lithography, HBM and DDR5 demand for AI servers, Cyclical capex patterns, and Increasing equipment intensity per wafer.
Representative participants: Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, Micron Technology, Kioxia, and Western Digital.
Integrated device manufacturers (IDMs) that design and fabricate their own chips, such as Texas Instruments, STMicroelectronics, and Infineon, account for about 15% of wafer manufacturing equipment demand. These companies focus on analog, power, RF, and embedded chips, often using mature nodes (28nm and above). Demand is driven by automotive electrification, industrial automation, and IoT, which require reliable, low-power semiconductors. IDMs are increasingly refreshing mature node equipment to improve throughput, energy efficiency, and compatibility with modern fab automation. Demand-side indicators include automotive production rates, industrial capex, and inventory levels.
While leading-edge IDMs like Intel invest in advanced nodes, most IDMs prioritize specialty technologies. Through 2035, IDMs will continue to invest in capacity for power semiconductors (SiC, GaN) and sensors, creating demand for deposition, etch, and cleaning tools tailored to these materials. Geopolitical pressures are also prompting IDMs to build regional capacity, supported by government incentives. This segment offers steady, less cyclical demand compared to foundry and memory. Current trend: Stable share, with focus on specialty and mature nodes.
Major trends: Automotive electrification driving power semiconductor demand, Mature node equipment refresh for efficiency, Regional capacity build-outs for supply chain resilience, Growth in SiC and GaN power devices, and Increasing sensor content in industrial and automotive.
Representative participants: Texas Instruments, STMicroelectronics, Infineon Technologies, NXP Semiconductors, and Analog Devices.
Outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) providers, such as ASE Technology, Amkor, and JCET, are increasingly important end-users of wafer manufacturing equipment, particularly for advanced packaging and wafer-level test. This segment accounts for about 10% of demand and is growing as chiplet and heterogeneous integration trends require more wafer-level processing steps before dicing. OSATs invest in deposition, etch, and cleaning tools for bumping, redistribution layers, and through-silicon vias. Demand-side indicators include advanced packaging capacity utilization, chiplet adoption rates, and smartphone and HPC shipment volumes.
Through 2035, the OSAT segment will benefit from the shift to 2.5D and 3D packaging, which demands high-precision equipment for wafer-level packaging. Additionally, the rise of fan-out wafer-level packaging (FOWLP) and system-in-package (SiP) modules will drive equipment demand. OSATs are also expanding in Southeast Asia and China, supported by government incentives. This segment offers growth opportunities for equipment suppliers that can provide cost-effective solutions for packaging applications. Current trend: Growing with advanced packaging and chiplet adoption.
Major trends: Chiplet and heterogeneous integration adoption, Fan-out wafer-level packaging growth, Through-silicon via demand for 3D stacking, Expansion in Southeast Asia and China, and Increasing wafer-level test complexity.

IMF: Bank of Japan to Raise Rates Gradually Toward Neutral as Growth Slows
The International Monetary Fund indicated on Tuesday that the Bank of Japan will likely lift interest rates in a gradual manner toward a neutral setting, even as growth in the country is expected to decelerate, according to Reuters. The assessment, published in the IMF's World Economic Outlook, places Japan alongside other central banks that are navigating inflationary pressures.
Japan's growth is projected to ease to 0.7% in 2026, with fiscal support measures partially offsetting the effects of higher energy prices, and to hold at that level in 2027 as the energy shock fades and monetary policy normalizes step by step. The 2026 forecast follows an expansion of 1.2% last year, and the IMF expects the economy to grow 0.7% in 2027.
The BOJ raised interest rates in September to 1.25%, a 31-year high, and signaled its willingness to continue tightening policy to guard against inflation exceeding its 2% target.
Japan's substantial dependence on imported fuel and raw materials leaves the economy especially exposed to the inflationary consequences of the energy shock and a weak currency.
Without naming any specific country, the IMF said monetary policy can see through the direct and near-term indirect effects on inflation only when the shock is temporary. Even in cases where such an approach is considered suitable, central banks may need to raise nominal interest rates if inflation expectations rise, so that real borrowing costs remain stable, the report stated.
The report also noted that exchange rates have seen significant volatility, particularly in Asia, leading some countries to intervene, including a joint operation by Japan and the United States to support the weakening yen. The IMF said preserving orderly adjustment and financial stability is essential while large shocks are playing out.
While economies should permit exchange rates to move flexibly to absorb external shocks, currency intervention becomes an option when market movements are disorderly, according to the IMF. It said temporary foreign exchange intervention can be considered where currency depreciation becomes self-reinforcing, market liquidity dries up, or currency movements threaten price stability through substantial pass-through or balance sheet stress.

articles.title: Japan September PPI Slows to 6.8%, Tempering Odds of Another BOJ Rate Hike This Month - bloomingbit
articles.summary: Japan September PPI Slows to 6.8%, Tempering Odds of Another BOJ Rate Hike This Month  bloomingbit
articles.full_text:
Summary
- September producer-price inflation slowed to 6.8%, fueling views that the Bank of Japan is unlikely to deliver an additional rate hike this month.
- Markets, based on pricing in overnight index swaps, see a high likelihood of one additional hike by January next year.
- With the Middle East conflict sustaining pressure from energy and raw-material prices and companies continuing to pass on higher costs, the BOJ’s future monetary policy is expected to depend on corporate cost burdens and the path of inflation.
Forecast Trend Report by Period
Japan’s producer-price inflation slowed in September, reinforcing expectations that the Bank of Japan will not rush to raise interest rates again this month.
Bloomberg reported on October 12 that the BOJ said its producer price index rose 6.8% in September from a year earlier. That was 0.8 percentage point lower than August’s 7.6% increase, marking the biggest slowdown since May 2025. On a month-over-month basis, the index fell 0.3%, matching the decline in August.
The slower increase in producer prices suggests some easing in companies’ raw-material procurement costs. Prices for agricultural, forestry and fishery products fell 13.3% from a year earlier, partly because of lower rice prices. The drop reflected a correction after rice prices surged last spring. Price growth for petroleum and coal products also slowed to 11.5%, helped by government subsidies.
The data have fueled views that the BOJ is unlikely to raise its benchmark rate for a second straight meeting at its October 30 policy meeting. The central bank raised rates last month, and the latest inflation figures reduced the need to rush into further tightening. Still, producer-price inflation remains high, making it difficult to say the BOJ’s rate-hike stance has ended.
Markets continue to anticipate another BOJ rate increase. Overnight index swap pricing shows investors see a strong chance of one additional hike by January next year, while many expect a move in December. With the Middle East conflict keeping pressure on energy and raw-material costs, companies are also continuing to pass those increases on through product prices.
Separately, the BOJ’s quarterly Tankan business survey released earlier this month showed companies’ long-term inflation expectations at 2.5%. That was slightly below the record 2.6% in the previous survey. Although inflation expectations have eased somewhat, they remain elevated, suggesting the BOJ’s next policy moves will depend on corporate cost pressures and the direction of prices.

About 1,200 students and parents attended admissions briefings for Seoul Semiconductor High School, which will recruit its first class of students next year. The school has only 64 places, yet each of the five briefings drew a steady stream of visitors. As expectations grow for jobs at large companies after graduation, high schools that train semiconductor specialists are drawing attention as a new path after middle school.
Chungbuk Semiconductor High School in Eumseong, North Chungcheong Province, the country's first Meister high school specializing in semiconductor equipment, is also attracting intense interest. About 1,800 middle school students and parents from across the country attended this year's admissions briefing at the school, which will select 96 students next year. That is roughly five times the 370 who attended last year. The New York Times' description of the school in June as the hottest high school in the country is also cited as a reason interest has grown.
Chungbuk Semiconductor High School maintains employment partnerships with more than 120 semiconductor companies, including Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, and has posted an employment rate above 95% every year. Seoul Semiconductor High School has signed memorandums of understanding with major companies including Samsung Display, Samsung SDI, Amkor Technology and Hana Micron, and employment commitments so far cover 217 positions. The school has set a goal of 100% employment after graduation.
The popularity of semiconductor high schools is spreading beyond the Seoul metropolitan area to the rest of the country. Yongin Semiconductor High School, which opens in March next year, closed applications for its August admissions briefing quickly, and the school fielded a stream of calls asking about dormitory arrangements and admission standards. The school plans to operate as a specialized vocational high school in the 2027 academic year before converting to a Meister high school from the 2028 academic year. Applications will be accepted online from the 3rd to the 5th of next month.
Daegu Semiconductor Meister High School has invested 30.1 billion won ($21 million) over the past four years to build semiconductor training facilities and a job placement office. The school runs tailored employment programs and provides all second-year students with 30 hours of hands-on training on the eight major semiconductor processes at the Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology (DGIST). It will recruit 96 students for the 2027 academic year, with applications accepted from the 19th to the 22nd of this month.
At Korea Semiconductor Meister High School in Gyeongju, North Gyeongsang Province, the ratio of applicants to places rose to 1.68 to 1 for the 2026 academic year from 0.92 to 1 for 2025. For the 2027 academic year, it will select 64 students across four classes in its semiconductor convergence department.
Interest is also building in North Jeolla Province ahead of a conversion to a semiconductor high school. Jeongeup Jeil High School, which will be renamed Jeonbuk Semiconductor High School next year under a provisional title, has been receiving dozens of admissions inquiries a day, prompting the school to assign two teachers solely to counseling. About 60 people have already signed up for an admissions briefing on the 17th, and the school expects around 200 visitors from across the country. Enrollment has filled only about 70% of available places each year, but the school expects the ratio of applicants to places to reach roughly 3 to 1 this year.
Incheon Semiconductor High School will hold school briefings on Nov. 7 and Nov. 21 as it begins recruiting students for the 2027 academic year. A briefing held in July drew 130 people, about twice the usual turnout. Selected by the Ministry of Education as a partnership-based specialized vocational high school, it has received 12 billion won ($8.4 million) in support over three years and will select 128 students next year.
Busan Electronics Technical High School plans to convert to Busan Semiconductor Meister High School, a provisional name, in March 2028. Its semiconductor department, which recruited its first class last year, recorded a ratio of 2.7 applicants per place, the highest among specialized vocational high school departments in Busan.
Chungnam Semiconductor Meister High School also drew about 180 students and parents to a recent admissions briefing. Second-year middle school students attended alongside third-year students. The school, converted in 2025 from the former Yesan Electronics Technical High School, teaches semiconductor manufacturing processes and equipment operation, and will select 48 students next year. Applications will be accepted from the 19th to the 22nd of this month.

(Oct 13): A global slide in semiconductor stocks deepened, sending South Korea’s chip-heavy equity benchmark down 7% as concerns about AI overheating and Chinese competition intensified.
Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc shares dropped more than 8% each Tuesday, weighing on the Kospi. A gauge of Chinese technology stocks tumbled 3.6% before paring its drop, while Japanese flash memory firm Kioxia Holdings Corp shed more than 12%. US chipmakers slumped overnight.
Investor angst over the AI trade intensified after Broadcom Inc’s chief executive likened market sentiment to a casino and warned that financing the buildout will become a key problem. That further undermined the case for AI stocks, just as higher interest rates begin to take a toll on massive debt-funded deals and threaten once-hot initial public offerings.
“Uncertainty over whether the upcycle can last into 2028 and beyond appears to be weighing on valuations and share prices” of Korean chipmakers, said Ha SeokKeun, chief investment officer at Eugene Asset Management.
Korean stocks took the biggest hit, as investors also reacted to a report that Chinese rival CXMT Corp has made progress on a new memory architecture that Samsung and SK Hynix are also working on. The Seoul stock exchange briefly halted Kospi program trading for the first time since August.
The Kospi is now down a third from the record high it reached in June. The benchmark has fallen below its 200-day moving average. Foreigners have accelerated their exit, selling more than US$6.3 billion (RM25.7 billion) worth of Kospi shares on a net basis in October.
CXMT plans to roll out a new server-memory product by the end of 2026 that enables higher storage density, according to a report from South China Morning Post on Monday. That resurfaced fears of rapid development by Chinese chipmakers that have rattled global rivals this year.
“Samsung’s strong earnings have been overshadowed by concerns about future competition from CXMT and the sustainability of AI spending,” said Jung In Yun, chief executive officer at Fibonacci Asset Management Global. “These concerns may weigh on sentiment, but CXMT still needs to translate technological progress into commercially competitive production at scale.”
Broader worry over the longevity of the AI boom continues to weigh on industry stocks after last week’s collapse of a planned offering by Nvidia Corp-backed data centre company Firmus Grid Ltd.
Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said financing may be a bigger problem than chip shortages. “A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in,” the head of the American chipmaker said at an event in Singapore. They “set very extreme expectations only to find out that it’s almost like they are in a casino.”
This week’s earnings from ASML Holding NV and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co will help investors gauge how long bumper profit growth can last. Shares of TSMC, Asia’s most-valuable company, slipped as much as 2% Tuesday.
Record earnings from Samsung last week failed to give the stock a boost.
“Traders aren’t treating good news stories or lofty valuations as gospel any more, they’re digging much more carefully into the numbers and the underlying business case, with the whole AI trade still under the microscope,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade.

Summary:
- Japan’s corporate goods price index rose 6.8% year on year in September, below the 7.6% forecast and August’s 7.6% gain, but still at an elevated level
- On the month, prices fell 0.3%, against expectations for a 0.5% rise, following a 0.2% decline in August
- Companies continued to pass on higher fuel and chemical costs to each other
- The yen-based import price index jumped 24.5% year on year, showing the weak currency is still pushing up the cost of raw material imports

Japan’s wholesale prices rose 6.8% in the year to September as companies passed on higher fuel and chemical costs, data released by the Bank of Japan showed on Tuesday, keeping inflationary pressure elevated and market expectations of a near-term interest rate hike alive.
The annual increase in the corporate goods price index, which tracks the prices companies charge each other for goods and services, fell short of the median market forecast of 7.6% and was below August’s 7.6% rise. On a monthly basis, prices fell 0.3%, against expectations for a 0.5% increase, after a 0.2% drop in August.
The headline miss offers the central bank only limited comfort. An annual pace near 7% remains well above levels consistent with the BOJ’s price goals, and the details point to continued cost pressure feeding through supply chains.
The clearest sign of that pressure came from import costs. The yen-based import price index surged 24.5% from a year earlier, showing that the currency’s weakness continues to inflate the cost of raw materials Japan brings in from abroad. With energy prices high, a soft yen magnifies the impact, raising the domestic cost of fuel and other inputs that companies then pass on to customers.
The data will be among the factors the BOJ board weighs when it produces fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts at its policy meeting later this month. Wholesale prices tend to lead consumer inflation, as firms gradually pass higher input costs on to households, which makes the pipeline readings an important guide for policymakers assessing whether inflation is becoming entrenched.
Markets will now focus on whether the BOJ uses its upcoming meeting to signal or deliver a further tightening step. A move that narrowed the interest rate gap with other major economies could help support the yen, easing one of the main sources of imported inflation. For now, the September figures suggest the softer headline reading has not changed the underlying picture of strong cost pressure.

articles.title: From Memory to Physical AI: Korea's Largest Chip Show Opens This Week - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: From Memory to Physical AI: Korea's Largest Chip Show Opens This Week  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
South Korea's largest semiconductor exhibition opens this week at its biggest scale yet, offering a single view of where the country's chip industry stands and where it is heading. Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK hynix (000660.KS) will unveil next-generation memory technologies for artificial intelligence, while domestic companies display capabilities spanning chip design, advanced packaging and physical AI semiconductors used in humanoid robots.
The Korea Semiconductor Industry Association said on the 12th that SEDEX 2026, the 28th Semiconductor Exhibition, will run for three days from the 14th to the 16th at COEX in Seoul's Gangnam district. Held under the theme "Into the Era of Silicon Intelligence," the show will feature 888 booths from 300 companies, including Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. That is about 70 more companies and 230 more booths than last year, making it the largest edition to date.
The main draw is next-generation memory technology for the AI era. As global investment in AI infrastructure expands, chips that improve data processing speed and power efficiency are becoming more important. That has pushed comprehensive competitiveness — combining memory technology with system chips and advanced packaging — to the center of industry discussion.
Samsung Electronics will present "AI System Design" as its core message, unveiling high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and next-generation three-dimensional memory technology. The company will also introduce a range of system chips, including mobile image sensors, processors and automotive semiconductors. It plans to highlight its technological capabilities for the AI era through integrated chip solutions covering memory, foundry services that handle chip design and contract manufacturing, and advanced packaging.
SK hynix will build its exhibition hall around the theme "An AI Journey That Keeps Moving Forward." Its featured technologies are HBM4E, the seventh generation of HBM, and high-bandwidth flash (HBF), a next-generation memory technology. HBF raises data processing bandwidth using NAND flash as its base and is drawing attention as a candidate to meet the AI systems' demand for handling large volumes of data. The company will also display core products including DRAM for servers, PCs and mobile devices, along with NAND flash and solid-state drives (SSDs).
Materials, components and equipment makers that underpin the industry's competitiveness will turn out in force. In chip design, ASICLAND, Chips&Media and OPENEDGES Technology will showcase their capabilities. Dongjin Semichem and MiCo will represent materials and components, while Jusung Engineering (036930.KS), SEMES and PSK will appear in the equipment category. In back-end processing and inspection, Hanmi Semiconductor (042700.KS) and EXICON will present the technological capabilities of the domestic chip ecosystem.
Another focus is the spread of AI technology into the physical world, including robotics. On opening day, An Hyun, president of SK hynix, will deliver a keynote address on the direction of memory innovation in the AI era. Shin Dong-ju, chief executive of Mobilint, will speak on the chip technologies required for the physical AI era, and Park Seung-bae, a professor at the State University of New York, will present on future computing technologies.
The exhibition will also host an international conference on advanced packaging research and development, a seminar on the semiconductor market outlook, and a global standards forum organized by JEDEC, the semiconductor standards body. On the final day, the 16th, a separate session will address semiconductors for humanoid robots — a look at how the use of AI chips is extending beyond data centers to robots and industrial sites.
The event also includes programs aimed at securing future talent for the industry. A job fair running for two days from the 15th will bring together 18 semiconductor companies and 433 job seekers. Attendees are expected to be able to explore key technologies and individual companies' business areas while also looking for employment opportunities.
"Semiconductors are the core foundation supporting an era in which AI extends into the physical world," said Park Gun-soo, vice chairman of the Korea Semiconductor Industry Association. "We hope students and job seekers who will lead the future chip industry will also visit the venue and see the era of silicon intelligence firsthand."

articles.full_text:
- $5 billion investment creates the world's largest semiconductor equipment and process technology R&D facility
- Purpose-built to accelerate the path from breakthrough innovation to high-volume manufacturing of next-generation chipmaking technologies
- Leading chipmakers, systems companies, equipment partners and research universities have committed to develop inside EPIC
SUNNYVALE, Calif., Oct. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Applied Materials, Inc., the leader in materials engineering for the semiconductor industry, today unveiled its Equipment and Process Innovation and Commercialization (EPIC) Center, a $5 billion capital investment* to build the world's largest facility dedicated to collaborative semiconductor process technology and manufacturing equipment R&D. Inside the EPIC Center, leading chipmakers, systems companies, equipment partners and university researchers will work side by side with Applied's scientists and engineers to accelerate the pace of chip innovation for the AI era.
"As AI infrastructure scales, the demands of high-performance computing are driving unprecedented complexity across the chipmaking roadmap," said Gary Dickerson, President and CEO of Applied Materials. "To win the race for AI leadership, our industry must rethink and re-engineer how we collaborate to develop and commercialize the next generation of semiconductor technologies. At EPIC, the world's leading chipmakers, system designers, equipment partners and researchers will work side by side with our teams to accelerate the path from breakthrough materials innovation to high-volume manufacturing faster than ever before."
Purpose-Built to Accelerate Innovation and Commercialization
Unveiled today at Applied's Sunnyvale, California, campus, the EPIC Center represents one of the most complex R&D construction projects in the world. The 600,000-square-foot structure houses nearly four acres of advanced cleanroom space and required more than six million construction hours to complete. Its foundation holds enough concrete to fill 34 Olympic-sized swimming pools, and its steel-reinforced structure holds enough steel to build two Eiffel Towers. Thirty-four roof trusses cover the cleanrooms, each spanning nearly 300 feet in length and weighing as much as 12 school buses.
EPIC is designed to reinvent the R&D model the industry has relied on for decades. In the traditional model, foundational materials research happens in one environment, equipment and process development in another, and process integration and pilot production in a third, with a careful handoff at every phase. The EPIC Center is designed to remove these handoffs, putting the people who invent the materials, build the equipment, and make the chips together in a state-of-the-art facility purpose-built for commercialization.

articles.title: Korea Risks Negative Growth From 2030 as Chip Boom Fades, Economists Warn - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: Korea Risks Negative Growth From 2030 as Chip Boom Fades, Economists Warn  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
South Korea's economy, projected to grow more than 3% this year on a semiconductor boom, could slip into negative growth from 2030, according to an analysis presented at an economic forum. Once the chip supercycle ends, economists warned, the underlying weakness of the economy will be laid bare. They called for reforms to foster creativity among Koreans and a shift in industrial policy to restore growth momentum.
Speaking at a forum titled "The Korean Economy: Where We Stand, Where We Must Go," co-hosted on the 12th by the Korea Development Institute (KDI), the NEAR Foundation and the Korean Economic Association at the Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Seoul, KDI research fellow Kim Mi-ru said the country's long-term growth rate has fallen by about 1 percentage point every five years since the early 1990s. "If this trend continues, it will enter the 0% range this year and could turn negative around 2030," she said.
Falling productivity was cited as the biggest factor behind the erosion of long-term growth capacity. Korea's average annual growth rate slowed to 3.1% in 2011-2019 from 4.7% in 2001-2010. Slower productivity gains accounted for 67% of that decline, the analysis showed.
The productivity slowdown is most evident in manufacturing, the mainstay of the Korean economy. Kwon Nam-hoon, president of the Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade, noted that exports from industries other than semiconductors and automobiles have been flat for about 15 years.
Participants said education that cultivates creativity is needed to strengthen the country's industrial competitiveness. "In the age of AI, the ability to think is critical to reversing the decline in long-term growth," KDI President Kim Se-jick said. "We must guarantee property rights and rewards for ideas, and build education and selection systems that develop creativity."
Others called for a change in the direction of industrial policy. Kwon proposed stabilizing supply chains, tailoring responses to the characteristics and circumstances of individual industries, and expanding ecosystems around key industries.
Kang Sung-jin, president of the Korean Economic Association, said growth strategy should focus on channeling accumulated industrial and research capabilities into economy-wide productivity gains and better quality of life. He stressed the need to redefine the roles of the market and the government.

Turnover has collapsed 70% from its peak in late May, foreigners are retreating at the fastest pace in Asia and local retail investors are also pulling back. The Kospi, the world’s best-performing major equities benchmark in the first half, has since lost 22% to be the worst in the second half while its AI-heavy Taiwanese and US peers set new highs.
Behind the reversal is a market whose AI fortunes hinge disproportionately on Samsung Electronics Co. and SK Hynix Inc., the two memory-chip giants at the heart of the global AI supply chain. That concentration is now a liability as investors question the durability of memory chips’ boom cycle, while the brutal leverage-driven selloff in the summer has made some global funds hesitant to return.
The two chipmakers together account for over half of Kospi’s weighting and powered its ascent earlier this year. Foreign funds pulled $131 billion from Korean stocks this year, the most among major Asian markets, according to exchange data compiled by Bloomberg.
Skepticism over memory chip demand was on full display when shares of Samsung, the world’s top producer of such semiconductors, fell Thursday despite a nearly nine-fold surge in quarterly operating profit.

“We have seen capital increasingly gravitate back toward US equities, contributing to ongoing foreign outflows from the Korean market,” said Richard Tang, head of research Hong Kong at Julius Baer.
Margin loans outstanding have hovered around 33 trillion won over the past month, after peaking at 38.6 trillion won in June, according to data from the Korea Financial Investment Association. Brokerage account balances — or investor deposits awaiting deployment — have also fallen to around 100 trillion won from a record of near 140 trillion won.

“The memory names in particular have become value names, cheap at current earnings,” said Jon Withaar, a portfolio manager at Pictet Asset Management in Singapore. “But retail and fast money hedge funds do not chase value or the concept ‘cheap’. They chase growth.”
To be sure, the declines have opened up buying opportunities for some investors who see AI spending and memory chip profitability still holding up. Korea’s ongoing initiative to boost corporate value is also another draw. Thanks to earlier gains, Kospi is still among the best performers for 2026 overall.
Yet for those less convinced, the competing Asian semiconductor hub of Taiwan is gaining favor due to its wider and deeper linkages across the AI supply chain and a more upbeat earnings outlook.
Up 70% this year, the Taiex Index beat the Kospi by about 23 percentage points last quarter, the widest margin since the turn of the century. Taiwan’s stock gains are also more broad-based, with about 10% of the local gauge’s members having at least doubled in value this year. That compares to 4.7% for Kospi.
“At this point in time, we prefer to express our tactical AI exposure through Taiwan equities, which offer a more complete technology hardware ecosystem and are supported by robust spending plans from major technology companies,” said Chun-Lai Wu, head of Asia Asset Allocation at UBS Global Wealth Management Chief Investment Office.

articles.title: Asian Technology Stocks Plunge as AI Investment Fears Hit Semiconductor Shares - Sri Lanka Guardian
articles.summary: Asian Technology Stocks Plunge as AI Investment Fears Hit Semiconductor Shares  Sri Lanka Guardian
articles.full_text:
Asian technology stocks fell sharply on Tuesday as a sell-off in US semiconductor shares spread across regional markets, with concerns about artificial intelligence investment, access to capital and intensifying competition from Chinese chipmakers weighing on investor sentiment.
South Korean memory chipmakers suffered some of the steepest declines. SK Hynix, a leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips used in artificial intelligence applications, plunged more than 8%, while Samsung Electronics fell 7.9%. Both shares reached their lowest intraday levels since August.
In Japan, SoftBank Group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry, dropped 8.03%, leading a broader retreat in technology and semiconductor-related stocks. Tokyo Electron, a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, fell 6.6%, while semiconductor testing equipment manufacturer Advantest declined 5.38%. Lasertec lost 4.76%, Disco fell 4.83% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.89%.
The regional losses followed a weak session on Wall Street on Monday, when the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.44%. US memory chipmaker Micron Technology declined 3.9% as investors assessed growing competition from China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), which reported progress in developing a new chip structure designed to increase memory density by storing more data in a smaller space.
CXMT announced the development over the weekend, intensifying concerns about the competitive position of established memory manufacturers. Its shares fell more than 2% on Tuesday.
Vey-Sern Ling, UBP’s senior equity adviser, said investors were taking profits on AI-related shares that had performed strongly during the year, particularly memory stocks.
“Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks,” Ling said.
He cautioned that Chinese memory manufacturers could eventually affect the global balance between supply and demand, but said they continued to face technological challenges, particularly in more advanced products such as HBM.
“In the short run they continue to face technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM,” he told CNBC.
Phillip Wool, chief market strategist at Rayliant Global Advisors, said CXMT’s progress represented a significant development for Chinese semiconductor manufacturers, demonstrating their ability to overcome technology restrictions and potentially challenge established competitors sooner than expected.
However, he said the market reaction appeared disproportionate to the immediate competitive threat because CXMT had yet to demonstrate large-scale production and continued to lag Samsung and SK Hynix in market share.
“More importantly, we’re not even talking about HBM here, and the Korean chipmakers are still unquestionably dominating that space, with very little threat at all from the likes of CXMT or anyone else for the foreseeable future,” Wool said.
He attributed the sharp declines to broader uncertainty about the sustainability of the AI investment boom rather than a fundamental change in the competitive position of established chipmakers.
“I read that more as a sign of how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment,” Wool said, adding that volatility could continue as investors reassess chip demand and the ability of semiconductor manufacturers to maintain their pricing power.
Concerns over financing have added to the uncertainty. The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could become a major constraint on the AI boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to exceed supply.
Investors are also awaiting a busy week of corporate earnings announcements and US inflation data, which could provide further indications of the economic outlook and the direction of interest rates. Higher interest rates can weigh on growth stocks by reducing the relative attractiveness of future earnings.
The latest sell-off reflects growing scrutiny of the AI sector’s investment requirements and competitive pressures as investors assess whether the demand for advanced computing infrastructure can sustain semiconductor companies’ recent gains.

articles.title: Why Gender Equality Could Be Asia's Best Defense Against Falling Birth Rates and Labor Gaps - Devdiscourse
articles.summary: Why Gender Equality Could Be Asia's Best Defense Against Falling Birth Rates and Labor Gaps  Devdiscourse
articles.full_text:
The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has warned that declining birth rates across Asia and the Pacific are exposing a deeper economic challenge: fewer children are not necessarily translating into greater participation of women in the workforce. In its October 2026 policy brief, Reassessing the Fertility–Labor Nexus: Why Gender Equality and Social Policy Matter, authored by ADB Gender Officer Fei Huang, the institution draws on international research and data from the World Bank, Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), International Labour Organization (ILO), and other institutions. The findings suggest that governments must rethink population policies, strengthen gender equality and expand social protection to prevent demographic decline from weakening economic growth.
The report examines fertility and employment trends between 1990 and 2023, challenging the conventional assumption that having fewer children automatically allows women to participate more actively in paid employment.
Global fertility is projected to decline to approximately 2.1 children per woman by the late 2040s. However, women's employment patterns differ significantly across income groups. While high-income economies generally maintained or increased female labor force participation, several developing economies experienced stagnation or declines despite rising incomes.
Thailand illustrates this contradiction. Its female labor force participation rate declined from 66.19% in 1990 to 59.29% in 2023, alongside falling fertility. China experienced a similar trend, raising concerns about the ability of rapidly aging economies to sustain their workforce.
Other Asian countries followed different trajectories. Pakistan's female labor participation increased from approximately 11.2% to 24.2%, while India and Indonesia recorded relatively limited fluctuations around 30% and 50%, respectively, over much of the period.
These differences suggest that economic development alone cannot remove barriers to women's employment. For governments, declining fertility without corresponding improvements in workforce participation could intensify labor shortages and constrain future economic potential.
The ADB identifies social protection as an important factor shaping the relationship between fertility and employment.
Across selected OECD countries, fertility ranged from approximately 1.3 to 2.3 children per woman in 1990, while female labor participation stood between 30% and 66%. By 2023, fertility had converged toward 1.1–1.7, while women's participation generally increased to approximately 40%–71%.
Nordic countries demonstrate how public policies can reduce conflicts between employment and family responsibilities. Subsidized childcare, paid parental leave, publicly supported services and incentives encouraging fathers to participate in caregiving have helped women maintain stronger connections with the labor market.
By contrast, Southern European economies, including Italy, Spain, Portugal and Greece, rely more heavily on family-based caregiving and generally exhibit lower fertility alongside comparatively weaker female labor participation.
The findings suggest that governments should prioritize comprehensive family support rather than rely exclusively on financial incentives to encourage childbirth.
East Asian economies are already confronting the consequences of exceptionally low fertility.
South Korea's fertility rate declined to 0.72 children per woman in 2023 before recovering slightly to approximately 0.75 in 2024. Japan recorded a fertility rate of around 1.2 in 2023 despite expanding childcare and family support measures.
China has introduced an annual childcare subsidy of CNY3,600 per child under three, covering up to three children. However, housing expenses, education costs, demanding employment conditions and unequal domestic responsibilities remain significant barriers.
The report highlights persistent inequalities in unpaid work. Chinese women spend 1.87 times as much time on unpaid responsibilities as men, while Indian women spend 3.3 times as much time on unpaid domestic work.
Such disparities restrict career progression, reduce employment opportunities and increase the difficulty of combining parenthood with professional responsibilities.
Technological disruption introduces additional challenges. Female-dominated occupations face approximately 29% exposure to generative artificial intelligence, compared with 16% for male-dominated occupations. Administrative, clerical and business-support roles are particularly vulnerable.
For employers, these developments strengthen the case for workforce training, flexible employment arrangements and policies supporting women's career continuity.
The ADB argues that demographic policies must extend beyond birth incentives to address the structural conditions affecting families.
Long commuting times, inadequate public transportation and limited access to childcare increase the burden on working parents. Governments should therefore integrate housing, transport and urban planning reforms with employment policies.
Affordable childcare, after-school services, flexible working hours and remote employment arrangements could help women remain economically active.
Social protection must also extend beyond formal employment. Across developing Asia, informal workers, self-employed individuals and digital platform workers frequently lack access to reliable family benefits and employment security.
The report recommends gradually expanding childcare, healthcare, eldercare and social assistance while strengthening workplace protections and opportunities for women in technical and managerial positions.
For development partners, these priorities create opportunities to support affordable care infrastructure, inclusive labor markets and sustainable urban development. Private businesses can contribute through workplace flexibility, employee training and family-friendly employment practices.
However, many Asian economies are aging before achieving high-income status, leaving governments with limited fiscal resources to finance comprehensive welfare systems. Carefully targeted and progressively expanded programs will therefore be essential.
That demographic resilience depends on treating fertility, employment and gender equality as interconnected economic priorities. Without coordinated reforms, countries risk facing shrinking populations alongside underutilized female workforces, placing additional pressure on productivity, household incomes and long-term development.

articles.title: Kyrgyzstan Approaches the Threshold of Demographic Aging - open.kg
articles.summary: Kyrgyzstan Approaches the Threshold of Demographic Aging  open.kg
articles.full_text:
The population of Kyrgyzstan has reached 7.4 million people, which is 70% more compared to 1990. However, behind this positive growth lie changes that could later affect the labor market, pension system, healthcare, and education. The rate of population growth is gradually slowing down, the share of children is decreasing, while the number of elderly citizens is increasing.
This was stated by Ajar Zholonbaeva, a candidate of economic sciences and acting associate professor at the Academy of Public Administration under the President of the Kyrgyz Republic named after Jusup Abdrakhmanov, at a media training for journalists held on October 12 by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) in Kyrgyzstan.
The expert relied on data from the National Statistical Committee, the 2022 population and housing census, as well as demographic forecasts from the UN presented in the World Population Prospects 2024 report.
Since the early 1990s, the population of the country has increased from 4.36 to 7.4 million people. It is important to understand not only the total number of residents but also the growth rates, which in recent years have fluctuated between 1.5-1.7%. Despite the positive dynamics compared to other countries experiencing population decline, Kyrgyzstan is seeing a noticeable slowdown in growth.
There is also a recorded decrease in the number of births: according to National Statistics data, about 140-141 thousand children are born annually in the country.
Zholonbaeva noted that a decrease in the number of births does not always indicate a decline in fertility, and it is necessary to consider the number of women of reproductive age and changes in the age structure of the population.
According to her data, the share of citizens under working age has decreased from 40% in 1990 to 33% by 2026, while the share of the working-age population has increased from 50% to 57%. The number of people over working age has remained at 10%, but in absolute terms, it has increased.
The expert emphasized that these changes could have long-term consequences. The reduction in the share of children in the future may slow down the replenishment of the labor force, while the increase in the number of elderly people will require new solutions in pension provision and social support.
These aspects need to be taken into account when developing educational infrastructure. Zholonbaeva suggested considering how the construction of new schools aligns with the projected number of children in various regions.
Although the population of Kyrgyzstan is relatively young, the country is gradually approaching the threshold of demographic aging.
By the beginning of 2026, the average age of residents will be 28.9 years. For men, this figure is 28.2 years, and for women, it is 30.1 years. The share of people over 65 years old is 6.4%, indicating an approach to the seven percent threshold according to UN classification.
An additional factor contributing to the increase in the elderly population is the retirement of people born in the 1960s.
Differences between men and women were also examined. In Kyrgyzstan, about 103-104 boys are born for every 100 girls, but the ratio changes with age. Among elderly women, there are almost twice as many as men, especially among those over 80 years old.
The life expectancy of women exceeds that of men by eight years. Zholonbaeva noted that this raises questions about the causes of higher male mortality and the factors affecting life expectancy.
According to statistics, in 2025, the mortality rate was 4.6 cases per thousand population, with 53.2% of all deaths caused by cardiovascular diseases. The maternal mortality rate is 22.1 cases per 100,000 live births, and the infant mortality rate is 11.6 cases per thousand live births.
Migration also remains an important factor in the demographic situation. Zholonbaeva noted that it is necessary to distinguish between permanent and current population. At the time of the 2022 census, about 1.1 million people were temporarily absent, of which 80% were abroad, mainly for work purposes.
In 2022, the urban population accounted for 34%, and by 2025, it is expected to increase to 42%. However, this growth does not always indicate accelerated urbanization, as it has been influenced by administrative changes.
According to UN forecasts, the population of Kyrgyzstan will continue to grow, although the growth rate will decline. An increase in the number of elderly citizens and changes in the age ratio are expected. Projections show that the working-age population will grow until the 2060s-2070s, after which it will stabilize. The share of youth and children, in turn, will decrease.
The expert emphasized that this demographic data should be used for planning state policy, taking into account changes in the age structure of the population.

articles.title: Samsung, SK hynix join US R&D hub as global chip leaders unite - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
articles.summary: Samsung, SK hynix join US R&D hub as global chip leaders unite - CHOSUNBIZ  Chosunbiz
articles.full_text:
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix will join the large research and development (R&D) hub that Applied Materials (AMAT), a global semiconductor equipment maker, has built in the United States. With TSMC, Intel and Micron also joining, a global collaboration system for developing next-generation semiconductor process and equipment technologies has been established.
AMAT on the 12th (local time) unveiled the EPIC Center, a joint semiconductor research and development facility, in Sunnyvale, California.
The EPIC Center is the world's largest joint semiconductor process and equipment research and development facility, with a total investment of $5 billion (about 6.6 trillion won). The total building area is about 55,700 square meters (about 16,800 pyeong), of which about 16,200 square meters (about 4,900 pyeong) has been built as a clean room for advanced semiconductor process research.
The EPIC Center is designed to carry out everything in one place, from semiconductor materials research to manufacturing equipment and process development to pilot production. By having chipmakers and equipment makers collaborate from the early stages of development, the goal is to shorten the development timeline for next-generation process technologies and speed their application to mass production.
As demand grows for performance and power efficiency in artificial intelligence (AI) chips, the complexity of fine processes and advanced packaging technologies is also increasing. Accordingly, the importance of joint research and development between chipmakers and equipment makers is rising, the explanation said.
Gary Dickerson, AMAT's chief executive officer (CEO), said, "The expansion of AI infrastructure and the resulting demand for high-performance computing are bringing unprecedented complexity across semiconductor manufacturing technology development," emphasizing the need for a new model of research and development collaboration.
Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, TSMC, Intel and Micron will participate as founding partners at the EPIC Center. Broadcom, Advantest, SCREEN, Kioxia and BESI, among other semiconductor design and equipment corporations, will join as innovation partners. Major U.S. universities, including Stanford and UC Berkeley, will also engage in research collaboration.
Korean semiconductor corporations also plan to use the EPIC Center to accelerate the acquisition of next-generation manufacturing technologies.
Song Jai-hyuk, Samsung Electronics' Device Solutions (DS) institutional sector chief technology officer (CTO), said, "Through EPIC, we will further accelerate the entire process from developing innovative technologies to advancing them and applying them in the real world."
Kwak Noh-jung, SK hynix president and CEO, said the company intends to respond to technology transitions in key memory products such as high-bandwidth memory (HBM), DRAM and NAND flash based on its collaboration with AMAT.
Wei Zhejia, TSMC's chairman and CEO, expressed expectations that the company will be able to secure next-generation semiconductor equipment technologies early and strengthen research and development in advanced packaging. Sanjay Mehrotra, Micron's chairman and CEO, likewise projected that the time from research and development of next-generation memory technologies to volume production could be shortened.
